# 2. The Python Visualization Ecosystem

**Matplotlib** is the low-level foundation and is commonly static-first. **Seaborn** builds statistical graphics on Matplotlib. **Plotly** and **Bokeh** make browser interaction—hover, zoom, selection and widgets—a central strength. Matplotlib can also use interactive backends, so “Matplotlib is never interactive” is not technically correct.

## 2.1. Matplotlib — Precise Figure Control

**Company question:** How is weekly revenue changing?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(1)
mat_df=pd.DataFrame({"week":np.arange(1,21)})
mat_df["revenue"]=85000+1800*mat_df["week"]+rng.normal(0,4500,20)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4))
ax.plot(mat_df["week"],mat_df["revenue"],marker="o")
ax.set(title="Weekly Revenue",xlabel="Week",ylabel="Revenue ($)")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Best for:** custom static analytical figures, reports, annotations and fine control.


## 2.2. Seaborn — Statistical Visualization

**Company question:** How does revenue differ across segments?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(2)
seg=rng.choice(["Consumer","SMB","Enterprise"],900,p=[.55,.3,.15])
base=pd.Series(seg).map({"Consumer":70,"SMB":125,"Enterprise":220}).to_numpy()
sns_df=pd.DataFrame({"segment":seg,"revenue":np.maximum(5,base+rng.normal(0,32,900))})
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5,4))
sns.boxplot(data=sns_df,x="segment",y="revenue",ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Monthly Revenue by Segment",ylabel="Revenue ($)")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Best for:** EDA, grouped distributions, statistical comparisons and regression views.


## 2.3. Plotly — Interactive Exploration

**Company question:** Which individual customers sit behind the overall pattern?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(3); n=650
px_df=pd.DataFrame({"customer_id":np.arange(10001,10001+n),"segment":rng.choice(["Consumer","SMB","Enterprise"],n,p=[.55,.3,.15]),"sessions":rng.poisson(9,n)+1,"tickets":rng.poisson(1.5,n)})
px_df["revenue"]=25+5.5*px_df["sessions"]+px_df["segment"].map({"Consumer":0,"SMB":40,"Enterprise":110})+rng.normal(0,25,n)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import plotly.express as px
fig=px.scatter(px_df,x="sessions",y="revenue",color="segment",size="tickets",hover_data=["customer_id"],title="Interactive Customer Explorer")
fig.show()
```

Hover, zoom, pan, select and toggle legend groups directly in the rendered chart.


## 2.4. Bokeh — Interactive Browser Plots

**Company question:** Can an analyst inspect and zoom into customers?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(4); n=500
bk_df=pd.DataFrame({"customer_id":np.arange(1,n+1),"sessions":rng.poisson(10,n)+1})
bk_df["revenue"]=(35+6*bk_df["sessions"]+rng.normal(0,30,n)).clip(5)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
from bokeh.plotting import figure,show
from bokeh.models import ColumnDataSource,HoverTool
source=ColumnDataSource(bk_df)
p=figure(width=800,height=380,title="Bokeh: Revenue vs Sessions",tools="pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset")
p.scatter(x="sessions",y="revenue",source=source,size=7,alpha=.45)
p.add_tools(HoverTool(tooltips=[("Customer","@customer_id"),("Revenue","@revenue{0.0}")]))
show(p)
```

Bokeh is especially useful for linked selections, widgets and browser applications.


# 3. Histogram — Distribution Shape

**Company question:** What does monthly customer revenue look like?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(10)
hist_df=pd.DataFrame({"revenue":rng.lognormal(4.35,.62,2500)})
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)); ax.hist(hist_df["revenue"],bins=38,edgecolor="white")
ax.set(title="Distribution of Monthly Revenue",xlabel="Revenue ($)",ylabel="Customers"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

<div class="viz-amber"><b>Bin width matters.</b> Too few bins hide structure; too many emphasize noise.</div>


# 4. KDE — Smooth Distribution Comparison

**Company question:** Do segments have differently shaped revenue distributions?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(11)
kde_df=pd.concat([pd.DataFrame({"segment":s,"revenue":rng.lognormal(mu,sd,700)}) for s,mu,sd in [("Consumer",4,.55),("SMB",4.55,.48),("Enterprise",5.25,.40)]],ignore_index=True)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)); sns.kdeplot(data=kde_df,x="revenue",hue="segment",common_norm=False,ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Revenue Density by Segment",xlabel="Revenue ($)"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

KDE is estimated smoothness. Do not interpret every bump as a real population mode.


# 5. ECDF — Cumulative Distribution

**Company question:** What fraction of each segment falls below a revenue threshold?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(12)
ecdf_df=pd.concat([pd.DataFrame({"segment":s,"revenue":np.maximum(5,rng.normal(c,c*.28,600))}) for s,c in [("Consumer",65),("SMB",125),("Enterprise",225)]],ignore_index=True)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)); sns.ecdfplot(data=ecdf_df,x="revenue",hue="segment",ax=ax)
ax.set(title="ECDF of Revenue by Segment",xlabel="Revenue ($)",ylabel="Fraction ≤ x"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The ECDF has no histogram-bin choice and makes percentile questions direct.


# 6. Box Plot — Compact Group Comparison

**Company question:** Which segment has the widest revenue distribution?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(13)
box_df=pd.DataFrame({"segment":np.repeat(["Consumer","SMB","Enterprise"],500)})
c=box_df["segment"].map({"Consumer":70,"SMB":130,"Enterprise":230}).to_numpy(); box_df["revenue"]=np.maximum(5,c+rng.normal(0,c*.25))
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5,4)); sns.boxplot(data=box_df,x="segment",y="revenue",ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Revenue by Segment",ylabel="Revenue ($)"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Box plots summarize median, quartiles, spread and potential outliers.


# 7. Violin + Strip — Shape and Observations

**Company question:** Do plans differ in the whole engagement distribution?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(14)
violin_df=pd.DataFrame({"plan":np.repeat(["Standard","Premium"],220),"engagement":np.r_[rng.beta(2.2,4,220),rng.beta(4,2.4,220)]})
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); sns.violinplot(data=violin_df,x="plan",y="engagement",inner=None,ax=ax); sns.stripplot(data=violin_df,x="plan",y="engagement",alpha=.28,size=2.5,ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Engagement Distribution by Plan"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Use violin plots when distribution shape itself matters.


# 8. Bar Plot — Categorical Summary

**Company question:** Which segment has the highest churn rate?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(15); n=2400
seg=rng.choice(["Consumer","SMB","Enterprise"],n,p=[.55,.3,.15]); prob=pd.Series(seg).map({"Consumer":.19,"SMB":.13,"Enterprise":.08}).to_numpy(); raw=pd.DataFrame({"segment":seg,"churn":rng.binomial(1,prob)}); bar_df=raw.groupby("segment",as_index=False).agg(churn_rate=("churn","mean"))
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); ax.bar(bar_df["segment"],bar_df["churn_rate"]); ax.set(title="Churn Rate by Segment",ylabel="Churn rate",ylim=(0,bar_df["churn_rate"].max()*1.25)); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

<div class="viz-red"><b>Bar lengths need an honest baseline.</b> Truncating the y-axis can exaggerate differences.</div>


# 9. Count Plot — Group Size

**Company question:** How many customers use each device?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(16)
count_df=pd.DataFrame({"device":rng.choice(["Web","iOS","Android"],1800,p=[.46,.28,.26]),"segment":rng.choice(["Consumer","SMB","Enterprise"],1800,p=[.56,.3,.14])})
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)); sns.countplot(data=count_df,x="device",hue="segment",ax=ax); ax.set(title="Customer Count by Device and Segment",ylabel="Customers"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Inspect sample size before interpreting subgroup metrics.


# 10. Scatter Plot — Numerical Relationship

**Company question:** Do more sessions correspond to more revenue?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(17); n=1300
scatter_df=pd.DataFrame({"sessions":rng.poisson(10,n)+1}); scatter_df["revenue"]=(30+6.2*scatter_df["sessions"]+rng.normal(0,32,n)).clip(5)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4.5)); ax.scatter(scatter_df["sessions"],scatter_df["revenue"],alpha=.25,s=18); ax.set(title="Sessions vs Monthly Revenue",xlabel="Sessions",ylabel="Revenue ($)"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Look for direction, curvature, clusters, changing variance and outliers.


# 11. Regression Plot — Average Trend

**Company question:** What average relationship is visible?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(18); n=900
reg_df=pd.DataFrame({"sessions":rng.uniform(1,25,n)}); reg_df["revenue"]=25+5.8*reg_df["sessions"]+rng.normal(0,28,n)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4.5)); sns.regplot(data=reg_df,x="sessions",y="revenue",scatter_kws={"alpha":.18,"s":18},ax=ax); ax.set_title("Average Revenue Trend with Sessions"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
A fitted trend summarizes association, not causation.
:::


# 12. Hexbin — Dense Relationships

**Company question:** How do two telemetry measures relate across 75,000 events?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(19); n=75000
hex_x=rng.normal(size=n); hex_y=.65*hex_x+rng.normal(0,.75,n)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,5)); hb=ax.hexbin(hex_x,hex_y,gridsize=45,mincnt=1); fig.colorbar(hb,ax=ax,label="Observations"); ax.set(title="Density Hidden by Overplotting",xlabel="Feature X",ylabel="Feature Y"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Use hexbin, density, sampling or rasterization when scatter points become an opaque cloud.


# 13. Line Plot — Change Over Time

**Company question:** Is revenue rising beneath daily noise?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(20); dates=pd.date_range("2026-01-01",periods=220,freq="D"); t=np.arange(220)
line_df=pd.DataFrame({"date":dates,"revenue":120000+180*t+10000*np.sin(2*np.pi*t/7)+rng.normal(0,6500,220)}); line_df["rolling_14d"]=line_df["revenue"].rolling(14).mean()
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,4)); ax.plot(line_df["date"],line_df["revenue"],alpha=.35,label="Daily"); ax.plot(line_df["date"],line_df["rolling_14d"],linewidth=2,label="14-day mean"); ax.set(title="Revenue: Noise vs Trend",ylabel="Revenue ($)"); ax.legend(); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Chronology is information. Keep time on an ordered axis.


# 14. Uncertainty Band — Show What We Do Not Know

**Company question:** Is a conversion trend larger than its uncertainty?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(21); w=np.arange(1,21); est=.12+.002*w+rng.normal(0,.004,20); se=np.linspace(.012,.006,20)
band_df=pd.DataFrame({"week":w,"estimate":est,"lower":est-1.96*se,"upper":est+1.96*se})
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)); ax.plot(band_df["week"],band_df["estimate"],linewidth=2); ax.fill_between(band_df["week"],band_df["lower"],band_df["upper"],alpha=.2); ax.set(title="Conversion Estimate with 95% Band",xlabel="Week",ylabel="Conversion rate"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Use uncertainty bands for forecasts, experiments and estimated quantities.


# 15. Error Bars — Experiment Estimates

**Company question:** How do A/B variants compare with uncertainty?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
exp_df=pd.DataFrame({"variant":["Control","Treatment A","Treatment B"],"conversion":[.100,.112,.107],"n":[12000,11850,12120]}); exp_df["se"]=np.sqrt(exp_df["conversion"]*(1-exp_df["conversion"])/exp_df["n"]); exp_df["ci95"]=1.96*exp_df["se"]
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); ax.errorbar(exp_df["variant"],exp_df["conversion"],yerr=exp_df["ci95"],fmt="o",capsize=5); ax.set(title="Conversion ± 95% Approximate CI",ylabel="Conversion rate"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Effect magnitude and uncertainty belong in the same comparison.


# 16. Correlation Heatmap — Matrix Pattern

**Company question:** Which numerical variables move together?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(22); n=1200
heat_df=pd.DataFrame({"sessions":rng.poisson(10,n)+1,"tenure":rng.integers(1,72,n),"tickets":rng.poisson(1.5,n)}); heat_df["revenue"]=25+6*heat_df["sessions"]+.6*heat_df["tenure"]+rng.normal(0,30,n); heat_df["satisfaction"]=np.clip(4.5-.28*heat_df["tickets"]+rng.normal(0,.5,n),1,5); corr=heat_df.corr(numeric_only=True)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,5)); sns.heatmap(corr,annot=True,fmt=".2f",center=0,ax=ax); ax.set_title("Correlation Matrix"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Correlation is a screening tool, not a causal map.


# 17. Pair Plot — Multivariate First Look

**Company question:** How do several customer measures relate at once?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(23); n=450
pair_df=pd.DataFrame({"segment":rng.choice(["Consumer","SMB","Enterprise"],n,p=[.55,.3,.15]),"sessions":rng.poisson(9,n)+1,"tenure":rng.integers(1,72,n),"satisfaction":np.clip(rng.normal(4,.65,n),1,5)}); pair_df["revenue"]=30+5.5*pair_df["sessions"]+pair_df["segment"].map({"Consumer":0,"SMB":40,"Enterprise":105})+rng.normal(0,25,n)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
g=sns.pairplot(pair_df,vars=["sessions","revenue","tenure","satisfaction"],hue="segment",corner=True); g.fig.suptitle("Multivariate Customer Overview",y=1.02); plt.show()
```

Pair plots are excellent for early EDA but become unwieldy as the number of variables grows.


# 18. Faceting — Small Multiples

**Company question:** Does a relationship change by segment?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(24); n=1000
facet_df=pd.DataFrame({"segment":rng.choice(["Consumer","SMB","Enterprise"],n,p=[.55,.3,.15]),"device":rng.choice(["Web","iOS","Android"],n),"sessions":rng.poisson(9,n)+1}); facet_df["revenue"]=25+5.8*facet_df["sessions"]+facet_df["segment"].map({"Consumer":0,"SMB":45,"Enterprise":110})+rng.normal(0,30,n)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
g=sns.relplot(data=facet_df,x="sessions",y="revenue",col="segment",hue="device",kind="scatter",alpha=.45,height=3.3); g.fig.suptitle("Sessions vs Revenue Across Segments",y=1.05); plt.show()
```

Small multiples often beat one overloaded plot with too many visual encodings.


# 19. Interactive Time Series — Zoom into Events

**Company question:** Can an analyst inspect a long timeline around an incident?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(27); dates=pd.date_range("2025-01-01",periods=420,freq="D"); t=np.arange(420)
its_df=pd.DataFrame({"date":dates,"revenue":100000+120*t+8000*np.sin(2*np.pi*t/7)+rng.normal(0,5500,420)}); its_df["rolling_21d"]=its_df["revenue"].rolling(21).mean()
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import plotly.express as px
fig=px.line(its_df,x="date",y=["revenue","rolling_21d"],title="Interactive Revenue Timeline"); fig.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True); fig.show()
```

The range slider and zoom controls are valuable for campaigns, incidents and long monitoring windows.


# 20. Confusion Matrix — Classification Errors

**Company question:** Is the churn model missing positives or generating false alarms?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(30); n=2500
cm_y=rng.binomial(1,.18,n); cm_score=np.clip(.12+.55*cm_y+rng.normal(0,.22,n),0,1); cm_pred=(cm_score>=.5).astype(int)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix,ConfusionMatrixDisplay
cm=confusion_matrix(cm_y,cm_pred); ConfusionMatrixDisplay(cm,display_labels=["No churn","Churn"]).plot(); plt.title("Churn Classifier: Confusion Matrix"); plt.show()
```

A confusion matrix shows *which kind* of error occurs, not merely how often the model is correct.


# 21. ROC Curve — Ranking Across Thresholds

**Company question:** How well does the classifier separate classes?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(31); n=2800
roc_y=rng.binomial(1,.20,n); roc_score=np.clip(.10+.60*roc_y+rng.normal(0,.24,n),0,1)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve,roc_auc_score
fpr,tpr,_=roc_curve(roc_y,roc_score); auc=roc_auc_score(roc_y,roc_score); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5,5)); ax.plot(fpr,tpr,label=f"AUC={auc:.3f}"); ax.plot([0,1],[0,1],linestyle="--"); ax.set(title="ROC Curve",xlabel="False Positive Rate",ylabel="True Positive Rate"); ax.legend(); plt.show()
```

ROC summarizes threshold-dependent ranking behavior.


# 22. Precision–Recall Curve — Rare Positive Classes

**Company question:** What tradeoff is available when positive cases are scarce?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(32); n=3500
pr_y=rng.binomial(1,.08,n); pr_score=np.clip(.05+.58*pr_y+rng.normal(0,.23,n),0,1)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve,average_precision_score
p,r,_=precision_recall_curve(pr_y,pr_score); ap=average_precision_score(pr_y,pr_score); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5,5)); ax.plot(r,p,label=f"AP={ap:.3f}"); ax.set(title="Precision–Recall Curve",xlabel="Recall",ylabel="Precision"); ax.legend(); plt.show()
```

Often more operationally revealing than accuracy for rare events such as fraud.


# 23. Calibration — Can We Trust 0.8?

**Company question:** Do predicted probabilities correspond to observed frequencies?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(33); n=4500
x=rng.normal(size=n); true_p=1/(1+np.exp(-1.3*x)); cal_y=rng.binomial(1,true_p); cal_score=np.clip(1/(1+np.exp(-.75*x)),.001,.999)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve
obs,pred=calibration_curve(cal_y,cal_score,n_bins=10); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5,5)); ax.plot(pred,obs,marker="o"); ax.plot([0,1],[0,1],linestyle="--"); ax.set(title="Calibration Plot",xlabel="Mean predicted probability",ylabel="Observed positive rate"); plt.show()
```

Ranking quality and probability calibration are different properties.


# 24. Residual Plot — Regression Diagnostics

**Company question:** Does prediction error change systematically?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(34); n=1200
actual=rng.normal(100,25,n); predicted=actual+.10*(actual-100)+rng.normal(0,12,n); resid_df=pd.DataFrame({"predicted":predicted,"residual":actual-predicted})
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4.5)); ax.scatter(resid_df["predicted"],resid_df["residual"],alpha=.28); ax.axhline(0,linestyle="--"); ax.set(title="Residual Plot",xlabel="Predicted",ylabel="Actual − Predicted"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Residuals can reveal bias, nonlinearity and changing variance hidden by a single RMSE.

# 27. Geographic Plot — When Location Matters

**Company question:** Where are orders concentrated around a service area?

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Data Simulator"
#| warning: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
rng=np.random.default_rng(35); n=500
geo_df=pd.DataFrame({"latitude":30.27+rng.normal(0,.055,n),"longitude":-97.74+rng.normal(0,.065,n),"orders":rng.poisson(5,n)+1})
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "View Plot Code"
#| warning: false

fig=px.scatter_map(geo_df,lat="latitude",lon="longitude",size="orders",hover_data=["orders"],zoom=9,height=500,title="Interactive Geographic Distribution of Orders"); fig.show()
```

Use a map when spatial relationships matter. If the question is only “which region is largest?”, a sorted bar chart may be clearer.

# 28. Other Modern Visualization Libraries

- **Altair** — declarative grammar-of-graphics and concise interactive statistical charts.
- **hvPlot / HoloViews** — high-level interactive plotting for DataFrame/xarray workflows.
- **Datashader** — rasterizes/aggregates huge datasets rather than drawing every point.
- **PyDeck / deck.gl ecosystem** — rich large-scale geospatial visualization.

<div class="viz-blue">The state of the art is not “use the newest library.” Match the tool to <b>data volume + analytical question + audience + interaction + deployment environment</b>.</div>

# 29. Which Library Should I Reach For?

| Need | Good starting choice |
|---|---|
| Custom static figure | Matplotlib |
| Statistical EDA | Seaborn |
| Publication/report control | Matplotlib |
| Interactive exploration | Plotly |
| Browser widgets / linked interaction | Bokeh |
| Declarative grammar | Altair |
| Huge point clouds | Datashader ecosystem |
| Interactive geospatial work | Plotly / PyDeck |

# 30. Visualization Mistakes That Mislead

- **Truncated bar axes** can exaggerate small differences.
- **Too many categories** turn legends into puzzles.
- **Dual y-axes** can manufacture apparent relationships through scaling.
- **Many-slice pie charts** make precise comparison difficult.
- **Rainbow scales** can create false perceptual boundaries.
- **Lines between unrelated categories** imply continuity that does not exist.
- **Means without uncertainty/sample size** can hide noise.
- **Overplotting** calls for transparency, sampling, hexbin, density or rasterization.

# 31. Exploratory vs Explanatory Visualization

**Exploratory:** “What is happening?” → many views, interaction, diagnostics.

**Explanatory:** “Here is what matters.” → fewer views, intentional ordering, annotation, uncertainty, restrained color.

<div class="viz-flow">EDA → DISCOVERY → ANALYSIS → DECISION → COMMUNICATION</div>

# 32. A Data Scientist's Plot Selector

```text
ONE NUMERIC → Histogram / KDE / ECDF / Box
NUMERIC + CATEGORY → Box / Violin / Bar + CI
TWO NUMERIC → Scatter / Regression / Hexbin
TIME → Line / Rolling trend / Uncertainty band
MATRIX → Heatmap
CLASSIFIER → Confusion / ROC / PR / Calibration
REGRESSION → Actual-vs-predicted / Residuals
LOCATION → Map only when spatial structure matters
```

# 33. A Company Visualization Workflow

If Product asks **“Why did conversion fall last month?”**:

1. Line plot → *when did it begin?*
2. Facets → *which device/segment/region?*
3. Funnel → *which stage?*
4. Distributions → *did population mix change?*
5. Event annotations → *what changed around that date?*
6. Statistical analysis → *is the change beyond noise?*
7. Explanatory chart → *communicate the finding.*

# 34. The Visualization Ladder

<div class="viz-flow">SEE → COMPARE → RELATE → SEGMENT → DIAGNOSE → EXPLORE → EXPLAIN → SHIP</div>

# 35. Final Perspective

<div class="viz-hero"><div class="big">✨ Choose the question first. Choose the plot second. Choose the library third.</div>

A sophisticated interactive chart cannot rescue the wrong visual encoding. A simple plot can reveal the entire story when it represents the right question.</div>

# Summary

- Distribution → histogram, KDE, ECDF, box, violin.
- Comparison → bars, box/violin, error bars, facets.
- Relationship → scatter, regression, hexbin.
- Time → line, rolling trend, uncertainty.
- Classification → confusion, ROC, PR, calibration.
- Regression → residual diagnostics.
- Plotly/Bokeh → browser-native exploration.
- Matplotlib/Seaborn → static-first analytical communication and statistical EDA.
- Every worked chart in this chapter has independently expandable **data simulator code** and **plot code**, with the visualization left visible.
